### 1.  Area of the spherical zone

The part of the sphere that lies between the two planes is a *spherical zone* (a band).  
A small element of the sphere at polar angle \(\theta\) (where \(z=R\cos\theta\)) has area  

\[
dA = 2\pi R\sin\theta\;(R\,d\theta)=2\pi R^{2}\sin\theta\,d\theta .
\]

Since \(dz = -R\sin\theta\,d\theta\), we have  

\[
dA = -2\pi R\,dz .
\]

Integrating from the lower plane \(z=z_2\) to the upper plane \(z=z_1\),

\[
S = \int_{z_2}^{z_1} 2\pi R\,dz = 2\pi R\,(z_1-z_2).
\]

With \(R=1\),

\[
\boxed{S = 2\pi\,(z_1-z_2)} .
\]

Thus the area depends only on the distance between the two planes, not on where the band lies on the sphere.

---

### 2.  Maximising the area

The distance between the planes is \(|z_1-z_2|\).  
Because each plane must intersect the sphere, we have \(|z_i|\le 1\). Hence

\[
z_1-z_2 \le 1-(-1)=2 .
\]

Equality occurs when one plane is at the “north‑pole’’ \((z_1=1)\) and the other at the “south‑pole’’ \((z_2=-1)\).  
If we require the planes to actually cut the interior (not just be tangent), the supremum of the distance is still \(2\); it can be approached arbitrarily closely.

Therefore the maximal possible surface area of the spherical part cut off by the two parallel planes is

\[
S_{\max}=2\pi\cdot 2 = 4\pi .
\]

---
